title: What a closed supervisory finding can tell us about a bank’s credit risk
summary: Closing a supervisory measure is an administrative event. Whether the bank resolved the underlying deficiency is a separate question. Alessandra Agati, Adele Fontana, João Matos Leite and Claudia Schwarz examine 8,106 credit-risk measures issued and closed between 2016 and 2025 in ECB Banking Supervision’s confidential records. Of the cases they could assess, 55.25% showed full remediation, 43.24% showed partial remediation and 1.51% showed none (Annex 1). The distinction matters for anyone using closure rates to evaluate supervision. Almost half the records document some progress without evidence that the original supervisory concern had been fully addressed.

The underlying database records what supervisors asked a bank to do and why they subsequently closed the measure. The researchers exclude procedural closures and cases with insufficient evidence. They use a language model to classify substantive outcomes from the description and closure narrative. Experts reviewed samples, the classification was run ten times with majority voting, and an alternative model agreed on about 90% of classifications (Technical Annex A). A second classification identifies the credit-risk issues involved. The exercise makes supervisors’ written assessments comparable across thousands of cases. It cannot establish whether different teams demanded equivalent evidence, whether remediation endured or whether borrowers’ realised losses fell.

Two empirical questions use different samples. Table 1 tests which features are associated with fully resolving a deficiency, using 6,969 measures with the necessary observations. Findings that span more topics have lower odds of full remediation. Classification and staging, governance and controls, provisioning and model risk, and credit lifecycle measures tend to do better than those concerning data, reporting or IT. For non-performing exposures and collateral management, the difference from the data and IT category is statistically inconclusive. Both high and very high severity predict less frequent full remediation than moderate severity. Non-binding recommendations more often achieve full remediation than obligations, but binding measures account for only about 6% of the sample and may be reserved for harder cases.

Table 2 considers elapsed time for 3,641 measures that achieved full remediation and have the required data. Each additional topic is associated with a 16% lower closure hazard, meaning a lower instantaneous rate of closure among the cases still open at a given time. Cases initiated through the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process have an estimated closure hazard 34% below those arising from on-site inspections. On-site cases also have higher odds of full remediation in Table 1. Inspections can yield more specific instructions, but supervisors choose their tools in light of the problem they face. These comparisons cannot identify the effect of substituting an inspection for another supervisory process. Legal enforceability shows no clear association with speed among the successfully remediated cases.

Weaker governance is associated with a lower chance of full remediation, yet the subset of successful cases at these banks can close faster. Selecting only successful cases can reconcile the two results. Several apparent relationships with bank characteristics also weaken once persistent differences across banks and supervisory teams are taken into account. The more stable findings concern the breadth, subject, severity and origin of the measure. The practical implication is that a short closure time is ambiguous without knowing what the bank had to repair, what evidence its supervisor accepted, and how many similar cases are still open. The most recent cohorts are especially exposed to selection because difficult measures have had less time to close.

questions.question: Does a classification of full remediation predict fewer repeat findings or better subsequent credit outcomes?
questions.detail: Follow comparable banks and credit portfolios after closure, distinguishing repeated deficiencies from changes in non-performing exposures and provisions. Independent follow-up assessments would show whether the narrative classification adds information about lasting improvement beyond the administrative event and whether that information is stronger for some topics than for others. Supervisory follow-up files and subsequent bank risk disclosures would help a credit analyst assess whether closure signals a durable change in portfolio risk.

questions.question: How do the results change when measures still open at the observation date enter the analysis?
questions.detail: Track all issued measures from inception, allow for censoring, and distinguish competing outcomes such as full remediation, partial closure and cancellation. Comparing cohorts at the same age could reveal whether the apparent improvement among recent measures survives once long-running data and reporting cases have had time to resolve. Comparing closure speed across banks for due diligence requires this denominator, which supervisory case registers can supply.

questions.question: Does the advantage associated with on-site inspections reflect clearer instructions or different initial deficiencies?
questions.detail: Within banks and closely matched severity and topic groups, compare the specificity of required actions, the evidence demanded at closure and subsequent re-opening. A blinded cross-team review of the closure documents could help separate genuine differences in remediation from different documentation standards. This matters before treating the observed ranking of supervisory processes as a guide for reallocating inspectors or interpreting a bank’s number of outstanding findings. Inspection reports, case files and follow-up reviews would be suitable primary materials.

limitation: The sample excludes ongoing measures and administrative closures. The duration analysis further conditions on successful remediation. Text classifications reflect the evidence recorded at closure, and supervisory tools are assigned according to risk rather than at random.
